key_terms.meaning: A policy enforcement point placed between networks that permits or drops each packet or connection according to an ordered rule set.
A firewall that judges each packet alone using header fields (source IP, destination IP, port, protocol) and keeps no memory of earlier packets.
A firewall that keeps a connection table, so a reply packet is allowed because it belongs to an already-permitted session.
A small network between the internet and the internal LAN where public servers sit, so a break-in there does not reach the LAN.
An IDS matches traffic against stored patterns of known attacks; good at known threats, blind to new ones.
An IDS learns a baseline of normal behaviour and alerts when current behaviour deviates beyond a threshold.
An intrusion prevention system sits on the traffic path and can drop or reset a connection, not only raise an alert.
A decoy host or service with no production role, whose only job is to attract, log and study attack traffic.
A network of honeypots plus controlled capture and containment devices, used to observe multi-step attacks.
Writing past the end of a fixed-size buffer, which can overwrite a saved return address and redirect execution to attacker code.
A random value placed before the saved return address; a changed canary on function return signals an overflow and the process aborts.
Virus (needs a host file), worm (self-propagating over the network), trojan (looks useful), rootkit (hides itself) and ransomware (encrypts data for payment).
A UNIX permission bit that makes a program run with the file owner's user ID, so ordinary users can use it for one privileged task.
The object holding a logged-on user's SID, group SIDs and privileges; every access check is made against this token.
A table with subjects as rows and objects as columns; each cell lists the operations that subject may perform on that object.
Permissions are granted to roles and users are assigned to roles, so rights follow the job and not the person.
Risk = Threat × Vulnerability × Impact, assessed qualitatively or in money, and reduced by controls until residual risk is acceptable.
An independent, evidence-based check that the controls stated in the policy actually exist and operate, usually against a standard such as ISO 27001.
In cloud, the provider secures physical plant, hypervisor and managed service internals; the customer secures its configurations, data, keys and identities.
Input deliberately perturbed by a small amount so that a trained model misclassifies it while a human sees nothing unusual.

takeaways: A firewall is only as good as its rule order and its default policy; the first matching rule wins, so put specific rules above general ones.
An IDS watches and alerts; an IPS sits inline and blocks, which also means a false positive can cut real traffic.
A honeypot has no legitimate users, so any traffic reaching it is suspicious by definition and cheap to investigate.
Memory-safety bugs such as buffer overflows are prevented by safer code, compiler checks and runtime defences such as ASLR and non-executable stacks.
UNIX and Windows both separate authentication (who you are) from authorization (what you may touch), and check permissions on every object access.
Access control models (matrix, ACL, capability, MAC, RBAC) are different ways to store and enforce the same question: may this subject do this operation on this object?
Risk management decides which control is worth its cost; a control that costs more than the loss it prevents is a bad control.
In cloud, almost every breach reported is a customer-side misconfiguration or stolen credential, not a broken hypervisor.
Machine learning helps security mainly by ranking and triage, and it fails when attackers poison training data or craft evasive inputs.
Every automated detector needs human review and a tuned threshold, because false positives cost analyst time and false negatives cost incidents.
bank_note: Long answers here are expected to compare mechanisms (stateless versus stateful firewall, IDS versus IPS, DAC versus MAC versus RBAC), draw the layered placement, and end with a control recommendation tied to risk and cost.

bank.q: Explain the four common firewall types — packet filter, stateful inspection, application proxy and next-generation firewall — and state one strength and one weakness of each.
outline: Layer at which each operates and what it can inspect
State kept per connection for stateful devices
Proxy terminates and re-originates connections
NGFW adds application identification and user identity
Cost and latency versus depth of inspection

bank.q: Define intrusion detection system and intrusion prevention system. List the four detection approaches (signature, anomaly, specification-based, host-based behaviour) with one example each.
outline: Detection versus prevention and placement
Signature store of known patterns
Baseline of normal behaviour and deviation
Rules derived from protocol specification
HIDS watches system calls, file integrity and logs

bank.q: What is a honeypot? Distinguish low-interaction from high-interaction honeypots, and explain how a honeynet adds value over a single honeypot.
outline: Decoy with no production use
Low-interaction emulates services only; high-interaction is a real host with containment
Risk of the honeypot being used to attack others
Honeynet captures multi-stage, multi-host campaigns
Legal and ethical limits on entrapment and data capture

bank.q: Describe the UNIX protection system: file permission bits, owner/group/other classes, and the setuid and setgid bits. Give one legitimate use and one abuse of setuid.
outline: rwx triplets for user, group, other
Directory execute bit meaning traverse
setuid runs with owner's ID
passwd changing its own file is a legitimate use
A root-owned setuid program with an input bug gives root shell

bank.q: A small office has one public web server, an internal LAN and a broadband link. Draw a firewall configuration with a DMZ and write the rule set (source, destination, port, action) needed to allow web access while blocking direct internet access to the LAN.
outline: Two firewalls or one firewall with three interfaces
Inbound 80/443 to the web server only
Web server may reach the database on one port only
LAN to internet allowed, established replies allowed back
Default deny on both directions, logging of drops

bank.q: A web server is being scanned and probed at night. Place an IDS/IPS and a honeypot in the DMZ and explain where each goes, what each logs, and what the analyst does with the output the next morning.
outline: IPS inline before the server, IDS on a span port
Honeypot on an unused address in the DMZ
Alert triage, correlation, false positive check
Block source at the firewall edge
Feed signatures and indicators back into the sensors

bank.q: Write a short C function that copies user input into a 64-byte local array. Show the unsafe version, the safe version, and the compiler and OS defences that would stop the unsafe version from being exploited.
outline: strcpy versus bounded copy with explicit size check
Stack layout: buffer, saved frame pointer, return address
Stack canary detection and abort
Non-executable stack, ASLR
Fortify source and compiler warnings

bank.q: Show how a role-based access control design is built for a college result-processing application with the roles clerk, faculty, examiner and administrator, then express one rule as an access control matrix entry.
outline: Objects: student record, marks sheet, result file, audit log
Operations: read, write, approve, publish
Role assignment and separation of duties
Matrix cell example, e.g. examiner may write marks but not publish
Least privilege and periodic review of role membership

bank.q: A team wants to move a payroll application to a public cloud. Using the shared responsibility model, list which controls stay with the provider and which the team must implement, and name three controls that are commonly misconfigured.
outline: Provider: physical, hypervisor, network fabric, managed database engine
Customer: IAM, data encryption and keys, patching of guest OS, network rules
Public storage bucket permissions
Over-permissive identity roles and long-lived keys
Open management ports and missing logging

bank.q: Compare a stateless packet filter and a stateful firewall for defending a campus network. Analyse how each handles a return packet of an FTP data connection established in active mode, and which one you would deploy at the internet edge.
outline: Rule matching on five-tuple only
Need to open a high port range if stateless
Connection table and sequence awareness in stateful
Attack surface created by wide-open port ranges
Recommendation with logging and default deny

bank.q: Evaluate the claim: 'An IPS is always better than an IDS.' Discuss false positives, inline latency, encrypted traffic, fail-open versus fail-closed behaviour, and tuning effort.
outline: Blocking decisions on wrong signatures cut business traffic
Inline latency and throughput cost
TLS hides payload unless terminated
Fail-open risk versus availability risk
Tuning, testing in detect-only mode first, and layered use of both

bank.q: Analyse how a machine-learning anomaly detector for network traffic can be attacked through data poisoning and evasion, and describe two defences with their limits.
outline: Training data collected from a compromised or unusual period
Slow, low-volume attack that becomes the learned baseline
Small perturbation of features to cross the decision boundary
Adversarial training and input validation
Drift monitoring, human review, ensemble and rule fallback

bank.q: A firm has a fixed security budget. Using risk management, explain how it should choose between a next-generation firewall, a 24x7 monitoring contract and an employee awareness programme, and state how residual risk is accepted and recorded.
outline: Asset identification and valuation
Threat and vulnerability assessment, likelihood and impact
Annual loss expectation for each option
Cost-benefit ratio and treatment options: mitigate, transfer, avoid, accept
Residual risk accepted in writing by the asset owner, with review date

bank.q: Compare the protection models of UNIX and Windows for a shared departmental server: user and group identifiers, permission checking on file open, privilege escalation paths, and vulnerability management practice.
outline: UNIX: uid/gid, nine permission bits plus ACLs, setuid binaries
Windows: SID, access token, security descriptor and discretionary ACL, integrity levels
Check at object open for both, cached handle afterwards
Privilege escalation: setuid mistakes, unquoted service paths, weak service permissions
Patch discipline, baseline hardening, audit of privileged actions

glossary.def: A device or software that enforces an ordered rule set on traffic crossing between two networks.
A firewall checks rules from the top and acts on the first rule that matches, so order changes meaning.
The policy that traffic is blocked unless a rule explicitly allows it.
A screened subnet holding public-facing servers, separated from the internal LAN by a firewall.
Firewall filtering that tracks each connection so replies to allowed sessions pass without new rules.
Intrusion detection system; a passive sensor that inspects traffic or host activity and raises alerts.
Intrusion prevention system; an inline sensor that can also drop or reset malicious traffic.
An alert raised on legitimate activity; it wastes analyst time and, in an IPS, can block real work.
A decoy system with no legitimate users, deployed to attract and record attacks.
A controlled network of honeypots with capture and containment, used to study attack campaigns.
A memory-safety bug where data is written beyond a buffer's bounds, corrupting adjacent memory.
Address space layout randomization; it loads code, stack and libraries at unpredictable addresses so a fixed jump target fails.
A random guard value checked on function return; if it changed, an overflow occurred and the program aborts.
Software written to harm or misuse a system, including viruses, worms, trojans, rootkits and ransomware.
A UNIX mode bit causing a program to run with the file owner's user ID rather than the caller's.
A Windows object carrying a process's user SID, group SIDs and privileges, used in every access check.
A subject-by-object table whose cells list permitted operations, the abstract basis of most access control models.
Role-based access control; permissions attach to roles and users attach to roles.
The principle that each subject gets only the rights needed for its task, for only as long as needed.
The chance and size of loss from a threat exploiting a vulnerability; often written Risk = Threat × Vulnerability × Impact.
The risk left after controls are applied, formally accepted by the asset owner.
A tamper-resistant record of security-relevant events used to detect, investigate and prove compliance.
The cloud split in which the provider secures the platform and the customer secures configuration, data and identities.
An input altered by a small perturbation so a trained model misclassifies it while humans see nothing odd.
Corrupting the training data of a model so it learns wrong behaviour or a hidden backdoor.
